reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Distinctive personality with an overly friendly, socially engaging manner and characteristic hypersociability
Recognisable elfin facies including a broad forehead, short nose with full nasal tip, wide mouth, full lips, and a small chin
Supravalvular aortic stenosis is the hallmark cardiovascular lesion, and other arteries including renal arteries may also narrow
Idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia may occur and requires attention to dietary calcium and vitamin D intake
Cognitive profile shows relative strength in language and social skills but marked weakness in visuospatial tasks
Caused by a microdeletion at 7q11.23 that includes the elastin (ELN) gene, explaining the arteriopathy
Connective tissue involvement contributes to hernias, joint problems, and a hoarse voice
Hypertension may develop over time and requires monitoring given the diffuse arteriopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Williams syndrome results from a recurrent hemizygous microdeletion of a contiguous set of genes at chromosome 7q11.23. Loss of one copy of the elastin gene (ELN) reduces elastin in arterial walls, producing the generalised arteriopathy and characteristic supravalvular aortic stenosis. Deletion of adjacent genes, including those involved in neurodevelopment such as GTF2I, contributes to the distinctive cognitive and behavioural profile. The deletion usually arises de novo through misalignment of low-copy repeats flanking the region during meiosis. Disturbed calcium regulation of uncertain mechanism accounts for the infantile hypercalcaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of supravalvular aortic stenosis such as familial ELN mutations
additionalInvestigations: Targeted testing for the 7q11.23 deletion, such as fluorescence in situ hybridisation or chromosomal microarray
Echocardiography and blood pressure assessment for cardiovascular involvement
Serum and urinary calcium studies to detect hypercalcaemia
Renal ultrasound and assessment for renal artery stenosis
redFlags: Severe or progressive supravalvular aortic stenosis with risk of sudden cardiac events, especially under anaesthesia
Hypertension from renal or diffuse arterial narrowing
Increased anaesthetic risk due to coronary and aortic involvement requiring specialist planning
reference.prognosis: Many individuals live into adulthood with support, but life expectancy and quality depend on the severity of cardiovascular disease; intellectual disability is usually mild to moderate and social strengths aid functioning.
pitfalls: Mistaking the friendly, verbal manner for higher overall cognitive ability than is present
Overlooking cardiovascular disease and the heightened anaesthetic risk
Failing to screen for and manage hypercalcaemia
Not monitoring for later hypertension and arterial complications
management: No treatment corrects the 7q11.23 microdeletion, so management is directed at the arteriopathy, hypercalcaemia and developmental profile
Cardiovascular management of supravalvular aortic stenosis and other arterial narrowings with blood pressure control and surgical relief of severe or progressive stenosis
Management of idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia by restricting dietary calcium and vitamin D intake
Developmental and behavioural support with early intervention, speech and language therapy and educational input tailored to the visuospatial weakness and hypersociability
Lifelong surveillance including echocardiography, blood pressure, renal ultrasound and renal artery assessment, serum calcium, hearing, vision and thyroid function
Heightened peri-anaesthetic vigilance given the risk of sudden death from coronary or biventricular outflow arteriopathy
Multidisciplinary care with cardiology, genetics and developmental paediatrics, plus genetic counselling as the deletion is usually de novo
